oil.summary: Crude caught a modest bid Thursday — WTI +1.73% to $71.52 and Brent +1.65% to $74.96 — but the recovery looks technical against a brutal monthly backdrop of roughly -24%. The dominant macro driver remains the Iran accord: the U.S. granted Tehran a 60-day sanctions waiver, nuclear inspectors have returned, and tankers are flowing freely through the Strait of Hormuz again. ADNOC's move to cut Murban OSP to $101.48 from $104.44 confirms Gulf producers are pricing in the supply re-entry. Middle East fuel oil exports are tracking toward a four-month high. On the other side of the ledger, Ukraine strikes continue to degrade Russian refinery capacity across 17 regions, offering a modest supply offset. RBOB lagged peers at -0.52%, consistent with the bearish demand-season read. CME options still price a 77% probability of a further OPEC cut at the next meeting.
drivers: Iran 60-day sanctions waiver and Hormuz reopening restoring tanker flows, pressuring medium-term price outlook
ADNOC cuts Murban OSP by ~$3/bbl, signaling Gulf producers adjusting to easing geopolitical risk premium
Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries in Krasnodar and Ufa tightening domestic Russian fuel supply, partially offsetting bearish global supply impulse

gas.summary: TTF slipped 2.71% on the day to €40.876/MWh, extending a -16% monthly decline as the Hormuz reopening narrative weighed heavily. The head of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum stated that markets are on course to rebalance in Q3 as Qatar restores LNG output — a direct bearish signal for European spot prices. ADNOC separately brought BP and TotalEnergies into Abu Dhabi's largest gas cap project, signaling continued upstream investment. Countervailing risks include a joint U.S.-Qatar warning to the EU that stricter methane regulations could exacerbate a gas crunch, and UK Energy Secretary Ed Miliband's veto of a Treasury plan to boost North Sea drilling for defense funding — removing a potential incremental supply source. President Trump publicly called out Exxon, Chevron, Shell, and BP over high fuel prices following recent market moves.
drivers: Qatar LNG output restoration post-Hormuz reopening driving GECF forecast of Q3 market rebalancing, pressuring TTF
U.S.-Qatar warning to EU on methane regulation risks introducing a policy-driven supply constraint to watch
UK Energy Secretary veto of North Sea drilling expansion removes a near-term upside supply catalyst for European gas

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs edged up 0.37% to $76.73, a modest but notable divergence from falling TTF gas prices, which typically act as a drag on carbon via reduced power-sector combustion demand. The week-on-week +1.79% and month-on-month +3.15% trend suggests EUAs are finding support independent of the gas selloff, possibly anchored by broader clean-energy policy momentum. Nine North Sea nations including the UK formalized a joint offshore clean energy initiative. On the demand side, Rystad projects the AI data center boom could drive the fuel cell market to $30 billion by 2030 as developers bypass congested grids. Global battery storage installations are accelerating, with Tesla securing a major multi-year utility-scale supply agreement. Ukraine's strike on Sevastopol causing a significant power outage adds a conflict-driven infrastructure risk dimension to the European power complex.
drivers: EUA carbon price holding positive momentum (+3.15% month-on-month) despite falling gas prices, supported by North Sea clean energy coalition policy signals
AI data center power demand surge underpinning fuel cell and battery storage investment, with Rystad flagging a potential $30bn fuel cell market by 2030
Ukraine strike on Sevastopol power infrastructure highlights ongoing physical risk to European grid security
